title: Major disruption as grass fire hits Heathrow train links
description: Trains to and from Heathrow Airport have been halted after a trackside grass fire caused delays and cancellations. National Rail said "major disruptio
body: Trains to and from Heathrow Airport have been halted after a trackside grass fire caused delays and cancellations. National Rail said "major disruption" was expected until the end of Saturday following the incident which began shortly after 16:00 BST.A statement said all lines were blocked between London Paddington station and Heathrow's terminals, as well as Reading, due to "a failure of the electricity supply caused by a fire next to the track".An update from Network Rail Western late on Saturday said the fire had been extinguished, but warned that disruption would continue, possibly into Sunday morning for some services.It comes hours after a separate grass fire on Heathrow's airfield shut a runway earlier on Saturday.Pictures on social media showed crowds of stranded passengers at Paddington, one of London's main rail hubs.London Fire Brigade said six fire engines and around 40 crew members were tackling the blaze near Scrubs Lane, North Kensington.Great Western Railway, external cancelled its services to Reading and no Elizabeth line or Heathrow Express services were running between Paddington and Heathrow on Saturday night.The airport advised passengers to leave extra time for their journeys, adding that the Piccadilly line, which runs services to the airport, also has delays.Network Rail Western said some services on Sunday morning could face delays and cancellations, caused by trains being displaced by the disruption. Earlier on Saturday, Heathrow's southern runway was closed while crews tackled a grass fire on the airfield. It caused some disruption with at least two flights diverted elsewhere. Heathrow apologised for any disruption and said the fire was extinguished quickly. That comes weeks after another grass fire near Heathrow's southern runway which forced 18 flights to divert and destroyed a large area of grassland. While weather has cooled across much of the UK in recent days following record-breaking heat over the summer, fire crews have still been warning of wildfire risks.The Met Office's Fire Severity Index, external shows that if a wildfire was to occur, it would have a "high" fire severity in most of south-east England and some of the Midlands.The fire severity is "exceptional", the highest level on the index, in some parts of London including Heathrow, as well as on the Essex and Suffolk coasts.

schema.headline: Major disruption as grass fire hits Heathrow train links

title: Prince William to attend King Harald's funeral in Norway
description: The Prince of Wales will attend the funeral of King Harald V of Norway on Wednesday in Oslo, Buckingham Palace has announced.Also going to the funeral
body: The Prince of Wales will attend the funeral of King Harald V of Norway on Wednesday in Oslo, Buckingham Palace has announced.Also going to the funeral, in a personal capacity, is Princess Anne, who is godmother to Norway's new monarch, King Haakon VIII.The late King Harald, a popular, modernising figure who had been on the Norwegian throne for 35 years, died last month at the age of 89.Royal sources say Prince William's attendance, representing his father King Charles, follows the convention that the monarch does not usually go to the funeral of another head of state.Large crowds are expected for the farewell to King Harald on 9 September, with a funeral procession to be followed by a service at Oslo Cathedral.Thousands have queued to pay their respects to the late king, during his lying in state in the chapel of the Royal Palace in the Norwegian capital.At the funeral, alongside Prince William, will be the widowed Queen Sonja, members of the Norwegian royal family including new King Haakon VIII, and other European royals.The service will be followed by a private burial in Norway's royal mausoleum in the Akershus Fortress.

schema.headline: Prince William to attend King Harald's funeral in Norway

title: Russia-Ukraine war: US envoys meet Putin in Moscow for Ukraine talks
description: US President Donald Trump's top negotiators have met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, as efforts to end the war in Ukraine gather pace.Foot
body: US President Donald Trump's top negotiators have met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, as efforts to end the war in Ukraine gather pace.Footage released by the Kremlin showed Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner being greeted by Putin, who said the current situation "is not so easy". Witkoff thanked Putin for agreeing with Ukraine to halt strikes on each other's capitals for three days. On Sunday the envoys will travel to Kyiv for more talks - their first such visit to Ukraine's capital.On Friday, Trump said Witkoff and Kushner were "bringing with them a proposal to end the war". So far, efforts by the US and its allies to broker a peace deal have failed.At Saturday's talks in the Kremlin, Putin also said that "whatever happens, such contacts are undoubtedly always useful". He also thanked Trump for his peacemaking efforts.He told the envoys that he was "comfortable" working with them, adding: "Of course on our side there is quite a high level of trust during this work."The talks – held behind closed doors in Putin's official residence in the heart of the Russian capital – lasted for three hours, according to Russian state media.Details are still emerging, but Putin adviser Yuri Ushakov described the talks as "constructive, extremely frank"."The talks were not limited to an exchange of views on resolving the Ukrainian crisis - economic issues and potential major, mutually beneficial Russian-American projects were discussed in considerable detail," he said.Ushakov also said "note was made of the Russian army's tangible advances in the combat zone" and that there was acknowledgement that talks needed to address "the root causes of the conflict".Despite an escalation of Russian missile and drone strikes on Ukrainian cities including Kyiv, Russian ground forces have made very slow advances for most of the conflict, incurring enormous casualties. Russia still controls about one-fifth of Ukrainian territory - areas that it seized back in 2022.Zelensky said earlier on Saturday that he had spoken to the envoys, who have "already begun working with the Russian side today". "The plan for tomorrow's diplomatic engagements in Kyiv, involving the US team, has been approved. We are waiting for Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and are ready for a substantive conversation," he added."From now through the end of Saturday, as well as on Sunday and Monday, Ukraine is ready to refrain from strikes on Moscow, and we expect the Russians to do the same regarding Kyiv."Russian state media reported that Putin had ordered a halt to strikes on Kyiv for three days due to the US visit.In televised remarks, Putin said Russia had not agreed to a ceasefire for the rest of Ukraine outside of the capital. The Russian president said he would "ensure the security of the negotiating process" and of the mediators.Kushner and Witkoff have visited Russia several times but the talks on Sunday would be the first in Ukraine. It is not clear how the US envoys will be travelling from Moscow to Kyiv.Ukraine's airspace has been closed since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.Delegations from Ukraine have attended talks in the US over the past 18 months.Earlier on Saturday, Zelensky said Russia had fired "demonstrative" strikes on airports in Kyiv and Boryspil overnight ahead of his planned meeting with the US.Ukraine's president added: "Clearly, these Russian strikes on the airports are a reaction to the discussions and preparations for the possibility of the US side using an aircraft to travel to Ukraine and land at Kyiv Airport or Boryspil Airport."Zelensky said on Friday he would guarantee the safety of Russian airspace during the envoys' visit and called for Russia to do the same for Ukraine.He also said an overnight Russian strike on a civilian building in the Dnipro region killed four people and injured five others.Witkoff and Kushner's visit to Moscow comes just over a week after a rare visit to the Russian capital by the head of the CIA, John Ratcliffe. There was no official comment from Washington or the Kremlin on what was discussed. Speaking last week, Trump described the meeting as "semi-routine".Last year, the US, Ukraine and Russia separately suggested that a deal to end the war was edging closer following a flurry of talks brokered by the Americans. European allies also held talks in Paris but discussions ultimately ended without a breakthrough. Key disagreements remain between the warring sides on issues such as territory and security guarantees for Ukraine. In recent months, both Russia and Ukraine have intensified their aerial attacks as fighting continues.Ukraine said it has struggled to repel ballistic missile attacks due to a lack of interceptor missiles, while Kyiv has focused its strikes on Russian economic infrastructure targets.

schema.headline: Russia-Ukraine war: US envoys meet Putin in Moscow for Ukraine talks

title: Taylor vs Pili: Boxing world pays tribute to 'one of the best to ever do it'
description: Former world champion Barry Jones picked out the final 20 seconds, when Taylor produced the kind of rapid combinations which defined so many of her bi
body: Former world champion Barry Jones picked out the final 20 seconds, when Taylor produced the kind of rapid combinations which defined so many of her biggest fights."That's what you really remember about her," he said on the Dazn broadcast."Those rallies of big punches, combinations and that's how she finished her last fight."American Mikaela Mayer - who was also ringside - was struck by the final image of Taylor placing her gloves in the centre of the ring."I was sitting there watching her put her gloves in the centre of the ring and it's like a story," she said.Taylor had long dreamed of fighting at Croke Park and had made clear she wanted the stadium to stage the final chapter of her career.Bellew said there was "no way" Taylor would return to boxing, although he could see her remaining involved by mentoring younger fighters."She will always be there to give her advice, speak to her and help her," he said."But ultimately she will sail off into the sunset and who could possibly deserve it more."

schema.headline: Taylor vs Pili: Boxing world pays tribute to 'one of the best to ever do it'

title: 'Fantastic' moment blind Abergavenny veteran, 95, drives again
description: 'Fantastic' moment blind veteran, 95, drives again after giving up licenceFigure caption, Behind the wheel at 90mph without a licence... or sightByNel
body: 'Fantastic' moment blind veteran, 95, drives again after giving up licenceFigure caption, Behind the wheel at 90mph without a licence... or sightByNelli BirdBBC WalesA 95 year-old veteran has spoken of his joy at driving again, five years after he was registered blind and had to give up his licence.Jim Alison, from Abergavenny, raced around Llandow Circuit in the Vale of the Glamorgan as part of a charity event which helps people with disabilities to experience driving."I think I managed to get to 90 km/h (55mph)," said Jim, a former chauffeur, who drove alongside an instructor with dual controls.  "You put your life in their hands and it was absolutely fantastic," added Jim, who served with the Royal Engineers for 22 years before becoming a driver in London.Image caption, Jim Alison used to drive for a living, but had to give up his licence as his eyesight deteriorated"They let me take over for a while going down the straight because, being sight impaired, I couldn't see the bends. "He said he never thought he would be able to drive again after his eyesight deteriorated due to macular degeneration.Jim was part of a group from Blind Veterans UK who took part in the Speed of Sight event at the circuit near Cowbridge, Vale of Glamorgan. The event allows people of all ages and backgrounds to experience the thrill of driving.Image caption, Some participants reached speeds of 60-70 mph on a damp day at Llandow CircuitHarley, 14, who has a visual impairment, went around the track for a second time, having first done so when he was 10."It's like happiness, excitement, wonder - it all goes through your mind in a blur because, literally, you're going so fast."He said it was a "good experience" for disabled children and adults, particularly those who love motorsports."You get a rush of adrenaline and you just feel really excited."Image source, Lesley MorrisImage caption, Harley said he felt a bit nervous before he got into the carSpeed of Sight is a charity founded by Mike Newman, a motorsports fan who was born blind and told his dreams of being a racing driver were impossible.But that did not stop him, going on to secure a number of world records for driving and in 2012 he set up his charity, a response to the many people he met who missed driving after having to give up their licences."Because I love cars so much myself, I tried to think of an idea of how we could get behind the wheel again and make it fun and exciting," said Mike."It opens up the opportunities of complete enjoyment, forgetting the day-to-day challenges that you're having to having to cope with."Or, if I can drive a car on a racetrack, what other things can be enjoyed."Image caption, Mike says the driving empowers people with disabilitiesThe cars used are modified Maxda MX5s with dual controls with names like Stanton and Baxter, a nod to some of the guide dogs which have lived with Mike over the years.Many of the participants are what the instructors jokingly call "repeat offenders", including Dean Twaite from Tredegar who drove army vehicles as a member of  Royal Corps of Transport in the 1970s and 1980s.Dean, 68, lost his sight in an industrial accident and has not had a driving licence since 2007."It was a bit frightening because I can't see in front of me. But the instructors, they were marvellous," said Dean, who explained he was given one tap on the leg to speed up and two to brake. "Feeling the wind in the face like that was exhilarating - it was really great, really great," added Dean, who said the experience brought back a freedom and confidence he couldn't describe"There's no such thing as can't. If you put your mind to it, you can do it."

schema.headline: 'Fantastic' moment blind Abergavenny veteran, 95, drives again

title: Katie Taylor vs Flora Pili: Ireland's boxing great crowns career in stylish Croke Park triumph
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Katie Taylor has won 26 of her 27 fights as a professionalByKal SajadBBC Sport boxing journalist at Croke Par
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Katie Taylor has won 26 of her 27 fights as a professionalByKal SajadBBC Sport boxing journalist at Croke Park, DublinKatie Taylor ended her illustrious career as a three-time undisputed world champion as Croke Park gave one of Ireland's greatest sporting figures the grandest of farewells on a night of celebration, spectacle and music.The 40-year-old outclassed unbeaten Flora Pili on points in front of 80,000 jubilant fans to add the vacant WBC belt to her WBA, WBO and IBF light-welterweight titles.With the footwork, speed and sharp pressure fighting that defined her career, Taylor produced one final stylish performance against the overmatched Frenchwoman to win by scores of 100-90, 100-90 and 98-91.Promoter Eddie Hearn paid tribute to Taylor, calling her "Ireland's greatest sportsperson", before she took one final lap of the ring, waving to the crowd before ceremonially placing her gloves and belts in the centre of the canvas.After almost a quarter of a century in the sport, Taylor - an Olympic champion, two-weight world champion and one of the pioneers of women's professional boxing - finally got her fairytale ending at her dream venue.She bows out with a record of 26 wins and just one defeat, but this was about more than one final result.It was a night steeped in Irish pride, with a spine-tingling atmosphere and chart-topping pop group Westlife helping provide a fitting send-off.Taylor in a world of her own in DublinImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Katie Taylor was roared on by over 80,000 fans at Croke ParkOn an unforgettable night for the city, around 80 per cent of those inside Croke Park had never previously attended a boxing event, but turned out to honour a fighter who dragged women's sport from the margins and took an entire nation on her journey.The crowd was the sixth largest recorded post-war attendance for a boxing event anywhere in the world. By early evening, the stands were awash with green and white, tricolours draped over shoulders.Westlife performed 'World of Our Own' and 'You Raise Me Up', with tens of thousands joining in as phone lights flickered around the towering tiers of Croke Park.The atmosphere softened for an a cappella version of 'Grace', the well-known Irish ballad linked to the 1916 Easter Rising, before the national anthem rang out.Chants of "Ole, Ole, Ole" drowned out Pili's ringwalk music before Taylor finally emerged to 'All Hail King Jesus', a nod to the faith she has spoken so openly about throughout her career.She stretched her arms wide, sang along and tried to take in every second of her final walk to the ring. There was emotion on her face, but also the familiar focus as fireworks shot into the Dublin sky.Taylor had spent fight week insisting there was still a job to do, but even for a fighter who had sold out Madison Square Garden and performed on some of boxing's grandest stages, it was hard to imagine her being untouched by a reception like this.Taylor puts on a show in finaleAfter a quiet opener, Taylor - who turned professional in 2016 - burst into life in the second round, firing quick combinations before darting back out of range.She repeatedly beat Pili to the punch, working in bursts and making the most of the two-minute rounds.Pili, 29, arrived unbeaten in 12 contests and had previously held the European title. With little expectation on her shoulders, she had everything to gain.But she had never faced anyone remotely close to Taylor's level and the gulf in class soon began to show.The party atmosphere continued between rounds as it became increasingly clear there would be no gatecrashing from the Frenchwoman.Former world champion Prince Naseem Hamed and UFC star Paddy Pimblett watched from ringside as Pili swung wildly in the fifth, only for Taylor to make her miss and fire back.Pili enjoyed her best spell in the seventh, a quick flurry briefly snapping Taylor's head back, but it did little to alter the direction of the fight.Croke Park rose for the final two minutes as Taylor continued to press forward, letting her hands go while the noise poured down from the stands.She embraced her mother, trainer and manager in the ring as 'Celebration' rang around Croke Park before the inevitable result was read out."Let me just look around for a second", she said afterwards, soaking up every ounce of the reception.'The greatest Irish sportsperson of all time'Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The last boxing event to take place at Croke Park was in 1972Taylor has been unequivocal that Croke Park would be the end and she walks away having beaten every opponent she faced as a professional.Her only defeat came against Chantelle Cameron in Dublin in 2023. Six months later, Taylor returned to the 3Arena and avenged it to become undisputed champion in a second weight division.After the final bell, she paid tribute to her family and somehow held the tears back as she spoke to the crowd."There's nothing like an Irish mammy," she said, smiling as she thanked those closest to her.For a fighter who has never hidden her dislike of media interviews, there was something striking about the confidence with which she walked around the ring, microphone in hand, soaking up the final moments."We did it. We brought boxing back to Croke Park. You were with me in London 2012, you were with me with the heartbreak of Rio. You stayed with me when I turned pro," Taylor said."I don't know any other country that would sell 80,000 tickets for a female athlete. I'm convinced Ireland is the only country."Taylor will forever be defined by her trilogy wins against Amanda Serrano and leaves with a staggering list of accolades, but her true impact cannot be measured in statistics alone.That legacy belongs to the young girl who once pretended to be a boy just to box when girls were not allowed.She fought tirelessly to get the sport sanctioned in Ireland and included in the Olympics, before going on to conquer both the amateur and professional codes.The belts will eventually gather dust, but the trail Taylor blazed across the sport will never fade.

schema.headline: Katie Taylor vs Flora Pili: Ireland's boxing great crowns career in stylish Croke Park triumph

title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong
description: The now widely used Mercator map was created in 1569 by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator.Its main purpose was to help European sailors navigate
body: The now widely used Mercator map was created in 1569 by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator.Its main purpose was to help European sailors navigate the oceans, as cartography Professor James Cheshire at University College London explained."He wanted a straight line to be drawn on a map to look like a straight line in reality if you followed a compass bearing," he told the BBC. "That was what it was intended to do, and that's what it does brilliantly well."To keep those angles correct on a flat map, Mercator had to stretch the grid lines wider as they moved away from the equator toward the poles.His map accommodates for the curvature of the Earth by making countries near the equator seem much smaller than they are, with countries nearer the poles appearing stretched.The distortion is a result of it being impossible to accurately represent the surface of a globe on a two-dimensional chart.More than 450 years on, Mercator's creation is still the basis for many of the maps we see in classrooms, on TV and online, including Google Maps.But critics of the Mercator map say there is a psychological effect to viewing some places as smaller than they actually are and others as larger, as we instinctively view bigger things as more important.For Kenyan geographer Kioko Muendo, this has implicitly downplayed Africa's vast resources, population and investment opportunities."Maps are more than just guides for travellers - they shape how regions are perceived politically and economically," he told the BBC.

schema.headline: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong

title: Man Utd can compete for major trophies says Michael Carrick
description: Manchester United believe they can challenge for major honours despite being unable to match the spending power of their rivals.United spent £148m on
body: Manchester United believe they can challenge for major honours despite being unable to match the spending power of their rivals.United spent £148m on new players this summer, less than newly promoted Ipswich, the £300m-plus invested by Chelsea and Tottenham and the record £458m spent by Manchester City.In their victory at Ipswich on Friday night, Liverpool fielded three players, Alexander Isak, Bradley Barcola and Florian Wirtz, who each cost more than £100m.By contrast, United's most expensive signing this summer was Cameroon midfielder Carlos Baleba from Brighton in a deal that could reach £70m, still £19m short of the club-record £89m they paid for Paul Pogba a decade ago.Head coach Michael Carrick says money in itself is not the answer to building a successful side and is adamant the club can compete."I certainly feel we can," he said. "The challenge is getting the right dynamics, the right balance and the right group together; getting the best players in the group to enhance the rest. Whether you need experience, or some younger players."There has been some criticism of United's transfer approach, with the lack of a left-back to compete with Luke Shaw and no striking support for Benjamin Sesko two areas highlighted.Carrick has rejected the notion restrictions have been placed on summer spending by United's hierarchy."The actual amount of money I understand can be a big thing but it doesn't always have to be the answer," he said.Has United's debt has restricted the club's spending power?Questions about that issue were raised at the Fans Forum at the end of June and respected finance blogger Swiss Ramble estimated in September 2025 that United had paid £852m in interest alone since the Glazer family's takeover in 2005.The club's latest quarterly figures showed total borrowings of £1.29bn, including outstanding transfer fees.United also took on an additional £91.92m when refinancing bonds in June and are yet to outline how they will fund a proposed new stadium expected to cost more than £2bn. The club's full year accounts to 30 June are due out in the next few weeks and will show the latest picture after a season without any European football.Against that backdrop, fans continue to protest against the Glazers at virtually every match. Yet chief executive Omar Berrada insists the club can remain competitive while managing its debt and stadium ambitions, arguing United's challenge is to operate sustainably while continuing to compete for major trophies."We have shown that with debt, we can not only [be] profitable, but more importantly, win trophies," Berrada told the club's Fans Forum on 30 July,. "And our aim is to do that again."Our role as management is to be able to operate competitively with a financial structure that's sustainable."We also aspire to build a new stadium, but we have to do it in a way that allows us to continue being competitive."We need to stay very disciplined and continue to take the right decisions on the pitch and put us in a position where we can do everything, where we can sustain the debt, aspire to build a new stadium and importantly, try to win as many trophies as we can."The arrivals of Baleba, Andrey Santos from Chelsea and Youri Tielemans from Aston Villa, plus the emergence of 19-year-old forward Shea Lacey leads Carrick to conclude his squad is in a better position now than when they ended last season, when they finished third after winning 12 of his 17 games in charge."Being at this club, you've got to strive to win," said Carrick."That's where we want to be, and we want to try and get to that on a consistent level."I don't like to keep looking back, but they know what it's taken to put that run together. Granted, there was one competition, and we need to do that an awful lot more this season, but we have strengthened the group, so we feel good about what's possible."Whether that optimism is justified will become clearer over the coming months, but Carrick believes United have assembled a squad capable of challenging despite spending significantly less than many of their rivals.

schema.headline: Man Utd can compete for major trophies says Michael Carrick

title: Nottingham Forest boss Oliver Glasner angry with VAR handball call
description: Nottingham Forest manager Oliver Glasner claimed the video assistant referee (VAR) was "guessing" and should not have intervened in ruling out Neco Wi
body: Nottingham Forest manager Oliver Glasner claimed the video assistant referee (VAR) was "guessing" and should not have intervened in ruling out Neco Williams' goal in their 0-0 draw with Tottenham.Williams' second-half effort was chalked off with the full-back adjudged to have bundled the ball in with his arm after some calamitous Tottenham defending at the City Ground.The Forest defender denied it came off his arm and insisted it should have stood.Initially, referee Craig Pawson awarded the goal but VAR Peter Bankes intervened."I watched five or six different angles and, to be fair, from one angle you can guess that the ball touched the arm because the shirt moves a little bit, but it's not clear is it the ball or [Sandro] Tonali on the goalline," said Glasner."I think the VAR can't intervene when he is guessing. It was not clear and obvious."We had a briefing before the season that the threshold for VAR intervention this year should be very high, which is why this is a wrong intervention."If it's not 100% clear, stick to the on-field decisions. This is the inconsistency today."I told the referee after the game that I felt the goal should have stood."The Premier League's official match centre posted on their X page, external the explanation as to why it was ruled out following the incident in the 67th minute.It stated: "VAR checked the referee's call of goal to Nottingham Forest - and determined that Williams handled the ball immediately before scoring and recommended that the goal was disallowed."The rule states that if the ball has hit the arm of the goalscorer immediately before they score then it must be ruled out, even if accidental.However, Williams denied that it struck his arm amid the chaos in the Spurs box."It's a goal," the Forest full-back told Sky Sports. "VAR is there when there is a clear and obvious error and for me that is not clear and obvious. I've seen the images and the replays and at not one moment did I think I handballed it. I headed it in between my arms."I knew straight away I've headed it down in between my arms. At a loss at that one. Disappointing."The biggest issue with judging handball is often determining if the ball did actually hit the arm, and that is the crux of Forest's argument.Williams is adamant the ball came off his head and did not touch his hand, evidence which of course would not be available to the VAR.Even having a chip in the ball, like at the World Cup, would not help here as the head and hands were so close together.This is not about a clear and obvious error, as that covers subjective incidents like potential penalties.It is a factual overturn so the VAR, Bankes, is looking for definitive proof. This is similar but without taking into account what the referee, Pawson, says he has seen.Definitive proof can be seen as a higher bar than clear and obvious, because it is a factual decision - that the ball definitely touched the goalscorer's arm.Glasner, Williams and most of the Forest fanbase refuse to accept that evidence does exist, and that there were no grounds to disallow the goal.These decisions come down to one factor - the judgement of who is in the VAR room on a given match.It is unavoidable that another VAR on a different day might feel the threshold of proof had not been crossed, and allow the goal to stand.And this will always be one of the major frustrations with VAR.Harry Maguire's goal against Ipswich last weekend was allowed despite a handball because his shot was going wide before it was deflected, meaning it was an own goal.In the Williams' case, he actually was the goalscorer so any touch on the arm means the goal must be ruled out.The only thing that would have saved the goal was if the ball had fully crossed the line before it was kicked against Williams.

schema.headline: Nottingham Forest boss Oliver Glasner angry with VAR handball call

title: Nigel Farage tells BBC he 'wasn't listening' in foreign donor talks
description: Nigel Farage has said he "frankly wasn't listening" during a conversation with his former chief of staff and an undercover reporter discussing what ap
body: Nigel Farage has said he "frankly wasn't listening" during a conversation with his former chief of staff and an undercover reporter discussing what appears to have been a scheme to funnel foreign money to Reform UK.His former chief of staff Dan Jukes and ex-head of policy James Orr have both been removed from their jobs after an investigation recorded them talking about how to get money to the party from an American donor and asking a fake company to pay for polling.Jukes has denied doing anything wrong. Orr has told Sky News he will co-operate fully with Reform's internal investigation.In an interview with the BBC, the Reform leader said he was not listening to the discussion and revealed his family are "begging" him to leave his job amid increasing pressure.In a film by Verbatim Investigations and Channel 4 News, Farage and Jukes were present during a conversation in which it is suggested the US donor gives £500,000 to Reform through his UK-based son.Under electoral law, donors to UK political parties must be a UK registered voter, or a company registered in the UK, so cannot give money from abroad through a British resident.The proposed donation was never made as it was part of an undercover sting, but that it was seemingly entertained has sparked questions.When asked about the exchange by reporters at Reform's party conference on Friday, Farage said he was questioning whether the arrangement was above board. In an interview to be broadcast on Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, he has now said: "I am not a compliance officer. I was in the middle of canvassing in the Clacton by-election. I turn up. I frankly wasn't even listening.""I was told there was a global family office based in London, so the money could have come from Singapore," he said of the conversation in the Channel 4 film."The money could come from all over the world, you know. Income could have came from all over the world into a family office based in London. I know electoral law. I know donation law better than anybody."Frankly, the two individuals involved here have never been involved in fundraising before and they shouldn't have been involved directly in fundraising. They should have done basic checks and nobody, nobody should be brought to me, unless they've been vetted from."The row over the Channel 4 film has threatened to capsize Reform's conference, with Labour and the Liberal Democrats calling on the Metropolitan Police to investigate the claims. The force is assessing whether or not to investigate. Jukes and Orr - both senior figures in Farage's inner circle - have stood down pending the outcome of the party's internal investigation, but political opponents are demanding that Farage is investigated and takes accountability.Farage categorically denied that Reform had ever taken money from a foreign entity by channelling it through a UK donor.But as pressure ramps up on Farage in the latest crisis to rock Reform, he also told the BBC that "for the first time", he does not have his family's support to be in politics. "They would rather I packed it up and walked away," he said. He added he had not considered standing down, but "when you've got your family begging you to, it's not easy". Farage also condemned the hundreds of masked "stop the boats" protesters who descended on the Port of Dover on Saturday morning, causing major travel disruption.Farage said he "deplored" anyone wearing masks or balaclavas at public demonstrations. He added: "You should not be allowed to be masked up, balaclava-ed up and go out and protest on the streets of our country. It is wrong at every level. So I deplore what is happening in Dover today."There's no question the allegations in the Channel 4 film have been embarrassing for Reform, and disrupted what they hoped would be a conference about their plans for office if they win the next General Election.Everywhere around the huge, draughty exhibition hall in Birmingham are giant posters and placards saying, "Reform - the first 100 days". They wanted to herald their deal with a serious contender to be the next French President, Jordan Bardella, to deal with small boats. They were keen to highlight the promise to cut income tax if they win the election, scheduled to be in 2029. They wanted to talk about their proposals for education, welfare, planning, and the rest. Party members, delighted to have a reason to get together, have taken part in those sessions, applauded and cheered in the hall; gone wild for Farage on stage. But for the rest of the country, most of the noise from the conference will have been the huge and awkward story about the toxic mix of politics and money.   What is harder to assess is the impact this mess will have on Farage's standing with the public, after a tricky summer and a recent poll slump.At the top of the party there is a quiet admission that what has happened here is a genuine mistake. One senior figure told me they could brush off other claims of murky funding, confident nothing had gone wrong - but they conceded these claims do matter, and that for a certain vital percentage of voters, it would "cause them to ask questions". No one is pretending it's just what Farage tried to joke was a "little, local difficulty". And there is a private acknowledgement that stories like this can be off putting to voters beyond Reform's no doubt very enthusiastic base.Another party source told me they were "totally blindsided" by the revelations; stunned "there'd just been no diligence" and in disbelief at how Jukes and Orr, who both say they'd done nothing wrong, seem to have behaved.A different member of the party's top team said, "hopefully, it's just growing pains". In other words, Reform's developed so fast that sometimes mistakes are made. But they told me: "The party has to step up – sometimes the people that got us here, aren't the people for the next stage". Among Farage's fans at the conference, I found different views. One member was convinced the party is treated unfairly: "It's the blob, it's all against him," she said. But another young Reform enthusiast rejected that, telling me: "It's all documented and there on camera – Nigel has to be more careful about what party members say." But there is a sense of "here we go again". When I asked another member what they thought of the financial scandal, a weary answer, "Which one?"This time last year in the same conference complex, Reform felt like they were simply sweeping all before them. Twelve months on, they are having to work harder, the scrutiny is more intense, and the pressure only growing. Farage's claim that he "wasn't listening" to the conversation was telling – to get to power without more of these kinds of serious embarrassments, he may have to pay more attention to what is going on.

schema.headline: Nigel Farage tells BBC he 'wasn't listening' in foreign donor talks

title: Sibling rivalry: When parents play financial favourites
description: 'My parents won't lend me £10k but helped my brother': When families play financial favouritesImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, One US study su
body: 'My parents won't lend me £10k but helped my brother': When families play financial favouritesImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, One US study suggests around 15% of siblings have had conflicts over moneyByDaniel ThomasBBC NewsDo your parents have a favourite child and give them more money, gifts or help?Financial favouritism can cause jealousy and resentment long into adulthood and, in some cases, even spark legal disputes after a parent dies. But experts say there are strategies that can help you avoid it.John says his parents, who have always supported his younger brother, recently refused to lend him £10,000 towards a house deposit after he broke up with his partner.This was despite the money being "well within their financial grasp", he says.His parents had previously given his brother a deposit to buy a home and subsidised his living expenses.John, 47, whose real name we have changed, says he was viewed as the more academic one growing up and expected to stand on his "own two feet" financially, while his brother, 42, struggled to make his way in the world and was "coddled".He says the favouritism has made him believe "the needs of others take precedence over my own", leaving him feeling "isolated" and affecting friendships and romantic relationships.'Powerful emotional meaning'Forums like Mumsnet and Reddit, external are full of posts complaining about siblings being shown preferential treatment regarding money. Common gripes include the amount of financial support adult children have received, external from their parents during their lifetime, the way inheritance is divided, external, and whether a sibling has supported their parents more than others, external.Dr Fenia Christodoulidi, from counselling service Relate, says that disagreements about money between siblings are rarely just about the money itself.  "Financial support from parents often carries a powerful emotional meaning and some siblings tend to interpret differences in support as signs of favouritism, unequal love or a lack of recognition." She adds that even when parents have "practical reasons" for treating their children differently, failing to communicate these clearly can "leave room for misunderstanding and resentment".Those reasons might include an adult child needing more support because they earn significantly less, have an illness, or have to pay more to get on the housing ladder due to rising prices, external.'It's never been a problem'Image caption, Ellis, 26, says there is no financial favourite in her familyEllis, who works in finance in London, tells the BBC that she and her siblings have had "different levels of support at different times" from their parents and it's never been a problem.Image caption, Tasha says her siblings have had disagreementsBut her colleague Tasha, the youngest of seven, says her siblings have fallen out over perceived favouritism, even though she thinks her parents treat them all the same."I just think people sometimes get a bit uncertain or jealous and that's quite normal," says the 33-year-old. "Sometimes people stop talking for a bit or go to process what they are feeling, and they come back together and they just hash it out."'Open conversations help'Having "open conversations about expectations and the reasons behind decisions" can help reduce feelings of resentment about money, Christodoulidi says.But for some, it's not that easy. "Talking about money is verboten in my family - be it salaries or savings or financial assistance," says John. "Any time I've tried to air my feelings my parents just become evasive so now I don't bother."John says he is now planning his financial future on the basis he won't have any inheritance - although he expects to be asked to step in if his parents get ill or lose capacity.He says he has a "great relationship with his brother" but feels resentment towards his parents for creating the "imbalance" between them.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Open conversations can help reduce feelings of resentmentClaire Webb, a solicitor and mediator at Family Solutions Now, regularly helps siblings who have disputes over inheritance and other money matters."One sibling might argue the other was given more money earlier on in life, say, to buy a house, and that the parents said this would be reflected in the will. "Then the will says, 'everything should be shared equally'. So you have all of that historic feeling of unfairness being dredged up."To avoid conflict, she says parents need to be clear with their children about what they want while they are still alive. 'A deep-down family bond'Siblings who do fall out should consider mediation before taking legal action, she adds. This is when a trained professional helps them remedy their problems.The good news is, siblings who take the legal route more often than not reach an amicable solution. "Most of the time there is a deep-down family bond - and if you can crack what started the problem they often find a way through."Tips for resolving money quarrels between siblings1. Recognise what's behind the row: It may be about feeling valued or treated fairly, rather than the money itself2. Avoid making assumptions about a sibling's financial situation or the reasons behind parental decisions3. Encourage open, respectful conversations where everyone has the opportunity to explain how they feel4. Parents should communicate their intentions as clearly as possible, particularly if they are supporting children differently for practical reasons5. Consider family counselling if conversations repeatedly become stuck or emotionally charged6. Consider mediation before taking legal action in inheritance disputes.  7. Choose powers of attorney carefully: Parents usually appoint their children to oversee their care and finances if they get ill or lose mental capacity. But if there's a risk they'll fall out, they can appoint someone else including a solicitor. Sources: Relate, Family Now Solutions

schema.headline: Sibling rivalry: When parents play financial favourites

title: Majority Russian-speaking city in Ukraine considers language ban in the arts
description: Ukraine's third-biggest city Odesa will decide this week whether to back a controversial plan to ban the Russian language in the arts.The proposal bei
body: Ukraine's third-biggest city Odesa will decide this week whether to back a controversial plan to ban the Russian language in the arts.The proposal being considered by councillors in Odesa on the Black Sea coast aims to add to existing restrictions on Russian imposed by national legislation. It is particularly significant because Odesa is overwhelmingly Russian-speaking, although the ban would only affect public spaces and everyday usage of Russian would remain unaffected.For millions of Ukrainians, Russian is their first language including many of the troops defending the country in its war with Russia. But Ukrainian is the only state language and spoken by the majority, and some see Russian as a tool of Russian influence.The proposal in Odesa, which is targeted daily by Russian drone and missile strikes, calls for a complete halt to Russian-language content in music and literature, in streets, parks, public institutions and state-run arts and entertainment venues. It would also recommend a ban in privately owned spaces.In a city famous for Russian-language writers and musicians, it has provoked strong passions. The ban would extend in public spaces to old Odesa songs almost universally known throughout the former Soviet Union. All Russian-language books would be removed from display in public libraries. Currently, they can be shown, but not prominently."The Russian language is a weapon of Russia, and we need to try to fix that," says Odesa lawyer Artem Kartashov, who has advised local authorities on an official programme to "decolonise" the city of its historic Russian legacy."With Russian-speaking music and other things, Russians try to deconstruct Ukrainian identity and influence especially young people, because they grow up in a Russian-speaking environment."But comic actor Borys Barsky, one of Odesa's best-known entertainers, says: "Russian isn't [only] the language of Putin, it's the language of [writers like] Dostoyevsky and Bulgakov. "Who benefits from setting people against other people who love Ukraine just as deeply, only love it in a different language? Only Putin benefits from this."Russian President Vladimir Putin has often referred to what he falsely describes as  repression of the Russian-speaking minority in Ukraine as one of his justifications for launching his invasion of the country.Russian and Ukrainian are closely related, but distinct in many ways. Many in Ukraine speak a mixture of the two, known as surzhyk. Russian is the native language of President Volodymyr Zelensky, which he used often in his election campaign but has since used only Ukrainian in public.But a 2019 law requires use of Ukrainian in many public and professional contexts including education, public services and customer service.Public-facing workers - including waiters, shop assistants and doctors - must address customers or patients initially in Ukrainian, though they can later switch to Russian if the client prefers that.Odesa's Mask Theatre, run by Barsky, has been fined for infringements of the legislation including using Russian in publicity materials. A later inspection found further violations such as a cafe sign with the Russian word for coffee."This isn't even like Orwell or Kafka, it's just madness," he says.Public playing of songs by Russian citizens is already illegal across Ukraine, with exceptions for some artists who have publicly condemned the war, but Russian-language songs composed or performed by Ukrainians are still allowed.Under the proposals they would also be banned in public places.  Anna Nerush said it would not affect someone celebrating their birthday in Russian in a private room in a restaurant, as it could not be heard outside. "But on the streets, [hearing] the Russian language can be a real trigger, for example to [former] prisoners of war and people who've come from occupied territories," she said.Many native Russian-speakers in Ukraine have switched to Ukrainian in recent years, particularly since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. Photographer Natalia Mykhailenko switched even earlier. She has led tours of Odesa highlighting non-Russian elements of its history. These include landmarks such as a Cossack cemetery that dates back to before 1794. That is the year Russian empress Catherine the Great is said to have founded the city, although it has been widely questioned in recent years.A statue of Catherine was removed from a central Odesa square after a council vote in 2022, and streets have been renamed to commemorate some Ukrainian writers and activists."We must understand we were a colony," said Mykhailenko. "And these [language] laws are very important. I understand it's maybe sometimes not democratic. But without it, there will be no normal Ukraine in the future."Anthropologist Anastasia Piliavsky, part of a group called Ukrainian Cosmopolis which aims to defend freedom of thought and speech, believes Russian-speakers are being made to feel like second-class citizens who are deprived of their heritage."In Ukraine, the vast majority of people understand both Russian and Ukrainian. So the question is not really one of language, it's one of liberty," she said."Ukraine has been fighting for freedom. The point of this war is not to be under authoritarian rule. That's what Russia has to offer. So when fines, or the threat of being fired [for breaking language laws] arrives, then people start wondering: what are we fighting for?"It is unclear how much support the new language proposal has. It is opposed by an influential group of councillors linked to former mayor Hennadiy Trukhanov.Beyond Odesa, a national poll showed 80% support for Ukrainian dominating "all spheres of communication" in 2022. However, a more recent survey of students in Kyiv found that 82% chose to speak Russian during break times, even though Ukrainian is enforced in classrooms.One famous Odesan who found himself at the centre of the language controversy is Pavlo Viktor, a physics teacher whose online lessons have been followed by millions around the world. Ukrainian language campaigners criticised him for putting the videos out in Russian, his first language, although he later translated them into Ukrainian. He was later criticised for saying he would talk to scared children in Russian during missile attacks, if that was the language they preferred.Viktor is keen to take the heat out of the argument, explaining that currently about 10% of the Odesa population spoke Ukrainian in the street: "But if we wait 50 years, maybe 90% will speak Ukrainian.""Ukrainianisation must be polite and soft… not to persuade children to move from Russian to Ukrainian, but to make an atmosphere when they want to do this. It's the best way. And I hope that gradually we'll move in that direction."You can hear more about the language controversy in  Odesa in the Crossing Continents podcast Ukraine: Fighting Russia, Fighting Russian, available from Tuesday 8 September.

schema.headline: Majority Russian-speaking city in Ukraine considers language ban in the arts

title: Italian Grand Prix: Pierre Gasly has George Russell covered at Monza in biggest surprise pole in years
description: A quarter of an hour before the qualifying session which delivered the biggest surprise pole position in Formula 1 for years, Alpine's Pierre Gasly wa
body: A quarter of an hour before the qualifying session which delivered the biggest surprise pole position in Formula 1 for years, Alpine's Pierre Gasly was playing online chess with Mercedes driver George Russell and winning."I must say before the quali, I felt pretty confident," the Frenchman said, "because I was picking piece by piece after piece."Gasly's performance coach Ben Thorne was watching."For a fun story," Gasly said, "Ben told me, 'OK, well, you're getting George here, but he's going to get you in a few minutes.'"Gasly said he reacted with a swear word but he was smiling as he recalled the moment."Turned out that it worked out well. So yeah, it's been fun," he added.Russell, who lines up second to Gasly, was laughing about it. "He beat me there," the Briton said, "and I thought, 'Well, I think I'll beat you in qualifying,' and here we are, he's ahead of me again."No-one - especially not Gasly nor his Alpine team - would have predicted the 30-year-old would end up on pole in Monza on Saturday, even though his only win in F1 came at this exact track six years ago.That victory, in the middle of F1's bizarre, spectator-less pandemic season, owed a lot to luck - a remarkable race that ended up with Gasly, then driving for Red Bull's Toro Rosso team, taking a restart from third place and Lance Stroll going off ahead of him on the first lap to gift him the lead once Lewis Hamilton had served a penalty.This pole was not like that. It was absolutely earned on merit.The Alpine has strong straight-line speed with a low-downforce-leaning aerodynamic design. The car - which has a Mercedes engine, the best in the field - has looked quick all weekend. It had an upgrade that lifted its performance at the last race in the Netherlands. And Gasly and his team absolutely nailed qualifying, while all the usual leading contenders had scrappy sessions one way or another."Monza is a bit of unique track as we know," Gasly said. "It definitely exceeded all our expectations."Since this morning, the pace has been better. We managed to make a good step from P3 to quali and I think slightly bigger than the other guys around us."Straight from Q1, we were a bit surprised to see us up there. Our target was Q3. But then I was P1 in Q1, then P4 in Q2. I didn't want to get too excited but then first run in Q3, I was third again."And then I felt, 'OK, well, I really have a shot at it.' It's probably the first time I really get a true chance and tried to leave everything I had out there."It was quite hectic through Ascari and Parabolica. I don't think there was definitely much (left) in there. And crossing the line, I knew it will be one of these laps that will be rewarded. But to the point to get to the pole position, I didn't expect that."Gasly is well liked within the paddock, and has many friends among the drivers, but he has long been one of F1's forgotten heroes, regardless of that win six years ago.A Red Bull protege, his time in the works team in 2019 did not work out. Like so many since, he was crushed by Max Verstappen, and demoted back to the second team after half a season.After sticking with Red Bull for three more years, he was given an opportunity with Alpine, and he hoped a move to a factory team would be his making.But Alpine have stumbled since, until finally showing signs of a revival this season, following Renault's decision to abandon its F1 engine project and switch to Mercedes customer engines.The team had been making headlines already this weekend.On Friday, Gasly lost the podium at Monaco to which he had been promoted after Alpine won an appeal against two penalties for pit-lane speeding, when the FIA court of appeal reinstated the punishment.A few hours later, de facto team boss Flavio Briatore caused an eruption in a news conference when he alleged one of the four judges in the case had "links" with McLaren.It was a claim that appeared to lack any substance, based as it was on a charity event in California in 2018 at which the judge in question had been present and to which a local McLaren garage had apparently donated "two or three" cars.And Briatore provided no evidence to back up the insinuation he was making.The claim was described as "insulting" in that news conference by McLaren team principal Andrea Stella, and afterwards it became clear that McLaren were furious about what Briatore had said on apparently the most flimsy of bases.Then, on Saturday, a rare statement from the FIA court of appeal refuted the allegation and any "questions (about) the independence and impartiality of the judges". The court of appeal verdict made a lot of sense. It left many questions about the controversy of the pit-lane penalties in Monaco, but at least it ensured all drivers who had been given them had been treated equitably - notwithstanding the fact that it seems none of them should have received the penalties.Regardless of the questionable nature of Briatore's comments, Alpine were unhappy about losing their Monaco podium, feeling that they had been given two penalties unjustly when their evidence showed Gasly had never been over the pit-lane speeding limit.Managing director Steve Nielsen told Sky Sports: "Two or three days ago, we were on the floor. It is really from being down to being on top of the world in just two days and it is amazing. We need to soak it up and make the best of it."Pierre is a class act. If you give him the machine, he will deliver. We failed to do that a few times last year."We haven't always given him the most competitive machinery this year, but when we have, he has delivered, particularly earlier in the season, So to see the team bounce back, to see him deliver on the track he knows well, he lives locally, he lives in Milan. It was wonderful."In qualifying, Gasly was positioned second last in the train of cars on the final qualifying run, the absolute optimum place in terms of a slipstream.Others, meanwhile, were compromised in one way or another, including the favourite for pole, Russell, when Verstappen disrupted Mercedes' attempts to have team-mate Kimi Antonelli tow the Briton by getting between the two silver cars at the end of their out laps."We had a bit of a mess with Verstappen entering the lap," Russell said. "He wanted to go for the tow, Kimi was there as well, and I did my lap a second and a half behind Max, which wasn't ideal."It takes nothing away from what Pierre achieved because, as he said, they were flying all day, quickest in Q1 and right up there from the beginning. So I'm happy for Pierre and, of course, disappointed we weren't on pole ourselves. However, great place to start for tomorrow."Russell acknowledged after qualifying what is at stake for him on Sunday. He goes into the race 59 championship points behind leader Antonelli, who has pretty much had his measure all season. But he has a golden opportunity to make up ground on the Italian, who is due to start 20th because of a grid penalty for exceeding his engine allowance.Russell said: "The win is going to be very important tomorrow but I'm more pleased about the performance. Since the summer break, every lap I have been in the top three positions, while I had that tough run of form before the break when every lap wasn't in the top five."Antonelli is expected easily to get back into the top six or so, but that would still allow Russell to make a substantial dent in his advantage.Given Russell has his own grid penalty looming within a couple of races for the same reason, it is imperative for his title hopes that he does so.On Friday, Gasly did not appear to have the race speed to challenge the top teams, so even though overtaking is harder at Monza than might be expected given its long straights, he knows it will be tough to win the race."Obviously not to the pace of these guys around us, but we seem to have picked up more pace from yesterday to today," Gasly said. "So we'll obviously give our best shot and see what we can get out of it."Aside from Gasly, Russell's main opposition is likely to come from Ferrari, who for the third race in a row seemed to fumble a better qualifying result for operational reasons. It was a bad time to do it again, as they debuted their upgraded engine at their home race.After both cars came perilously close to being knocked out in the second part of qualifying, Charles Leclerc left the pits in the final session while Lewis Hamilton had no wheels on his car, so the seven-time champion was far from best placed for his run in terms of the slipstream.Leclerc and Hamilton will start third and fourth after McLaren's Oscar Piastri was given a three-place grid penalty for impeding Red Bull's Liam Lawson.Hamilton - like Russell, 59 points behind Antonelli - seemed to imply after qualifying that he felt the team should prioritise his hopes over Leclerc's, even if he could not quite bring himself to say it outright."(Piastri's penalty) puts us in (with a) fighting chance, hopefully, with George," Hamilton said. "That's one Mercedes up front, so hopefully that gives us a chance to work as a team to try and topple them."We're at a point in the year where 59 points is a huge - huge - deficit to recover from, especially when Mercedes continue to be the leaders in speed."So yeah, we do have to work as a team. Have we been...  if and when that would ever change... we'll find out, but all I can do is just try to arrive and do the best job I can."

schema.headline: Italian Grand Prix: Pierre Gasly has George Russell covered at Monza in biggest surprise pole in years

title: Why more women carry the 'mental load' - and how couples can share it
description: Image source, Halfpoint ImagesByGrace Dean and Mallory Moench"My head's always full," says mum-of-three Stacie Matthias. "I go to sleep with a mental
body: Image source, Halfpoint ImagesByGrace Dean and Mallory Moench"My head's always full," says mum-of-three Stacie Matthias. "I go to sleep with a mental to-do list."She's talking about the concept of the "mental load" - the burden of planning, organising, remembering and anticipating tasks that keep a household running.These tasks include: remembering school trips, checking for updates in parents' WhatsApp groups, noticing which parts of the house need cleaning, monitoring how much sleep children get, scheduling doctors' appointments and buying school uniforms.According to academics, this is work that in heterosexual couples disproportionately falls to women - particularly mothers - alongside the bulk of physical household labour.All relationships and households are different, of course, but studies suggest clear patterns.Children in the UK have just gone back to school from the summer holidays, and Stacie, 37, from Stockport, says her mind often feels especially busy in September."It's that feeling of always having something to remember, organise or worry about that makes this time of year particularly full-on," she says.For Stacie this list of responsibilities leaves her mind feeling like a washing-up bowl that's being filled up throughout the day. "If someone's not helping you remove those pots and pans, your water's overflowing by the end of the day," she says, "and you're at tipping point."Image source, Stacie MatthiasImage caption, Stacie says she always has something to "remember, organise or worry about"In a survey looking into the mental load that involved 3,000 US parents, academics at the University of Bath and the University of Melbourne , externalfound that mothers handled 71% of household tasks that required mental effort, such as keeping track of when sheets and towels needed to be washed and remembering by when food in the fridge needed to be eaten.The study found that fathers handled many of the tasks researchers described as "episodic" - things that happen less often, such as remembering when to get the car serviced.University of Melbourne Prof Leah Ruppaner describes the mental load as being invisible, enduring and without boundaries. "You don't bring your dishes to work, but you bring the mental load everywhere," she says.The mental load is a popular topic on forums like Reddit and Mumsnet, where women seek advice about how to talk to their partners about the exhaustion of trying to juggle so many different responsibilities.Mums told BBC News they were often added to school WhatsApp groups - where parents discuss things like non-uniform days, school trips, birthdays and lost property - as the "default parent", while their partners never joined.Sophia, a 35-year-old mum of three in Portsmouth, pays for school trips and makes lunch orders on her children's school's app on her phone, but says her husband has never downloaded it.Sophia says she tried multiple times to explain the concept of the mental load to her husband - but feels he didn't understand and dismissed her concerns as "quick tasks"."They are quick tasks if you could just do the task," Sophia says, "but I have to plan for the task, I have to anticipate the task, I have to be 10 steps ahead all the time."Image source, Getty ImagesSam Berry, a deputy headteacher, content creator and married dad of two in London, says when his wife first raised the idea of mental load after his eldest was born, he "didn't really get it" and was "a bit defensive" because he thought he was doing a lot - changing nappies, feeding the baby and more.He would ask what he could do to help, but he says that still puts the burden on the other person to do the thinking.As Stacie explains: "I always say to my partner: 'If I have to ask you to do something, that's just adding to my mental load'."It took a few months of talking and listening for Sam to understand that it was not only about completing the task, but the thinking around it - not just cooking dinner, but what food was in the house, planning the meal, and doing the shopping.Clinical psychologist Natasha Wallace says some women come to her feeling stressed by the pressure they feel to organise their households."It's often, for them, not one enormous stressor," she says. "It's when they realise that they have hundreds of tiny demands on them and their brains and bodies just can't switch off."Many women are running on autopilot, she adds, so they often don't realise the extent of the cognitive load they're carrying, and this constant low-level stress can have an effect on the nervous system. In turn, this can cause poor sleep, irritability and decision fatigue, she says.Image source, Natasha WallaceImage caption, Wallace says being constantly stressed can impact mental health and restAnita Cleare, parenting expert and author of The Work/Parent Switch, said the overall cognitive drain spills over into our work lives and leads to unsustainable burnout.One piece of research found , externalthat men who earned more did less physical and cognitive labour related to the household, but that when women's earnings increase, they do less physical housework but still the same amount of cognitive labour.Women very seldomly feel it is a choice to opt out of family life, so the choice then becomes whether to decelerate their career, go part-time, or stop and stay home - with more and more women making that decision, Cleare says."If you lower the domestic load, if you lower the mental load, you will create energy, capacity, interest in being able to perform more and better at work."Why the disparity?Many of the women the BBC interviewed said they believed the disparity began with maternity leave.Wallace says that because women typically take much longer for maternity leave than dads do for paternity leave, they become the "default parent" very early on."If you become the person who knows everything, knows where everything is and has in the past done everything, everybody starts coming to you for everything," she says, "so you remain that central person even if you return to work."In the UK, mothers can take up to 52 weeks of statutory maternity leave, 39 of which can be paid, while fathers can take up to two weeks of leave with statutory paternity pay. Parents can also take shared parental leave.Some employers offer extra parental leave to their workers, but most people earn less when on maternity or paternity leave, which affects how much leave many fathers take.Cleare says workplaces can help by making examples of fathers taking paternity leave, not just offering it, and by setting expectations around when employees are contactable, and supporting career conversations for women.It can also come down to what are seen as traditional roles.Zach Watson, a married father of three and coach in the US on sharing the mental load, says his grandfather might never have cooked a meal in his married life, while his father did only a little.In the first five years of his marriage, his wife cooked most of the time. If he offered to cook, he would ask her what she wanted - a question that could actually add to her mental load.He learned he could come to her with options for dinner, having already looked in the fridge, and give her a default if she wanted to opt entirely out of decision-making. And if he needed help, instead of just asking "Where's the ketchup?", he could explain where he had already looked.Image source, Maskot/Getty ImagesImage caption, Women say it's crucial that their partners take full ownership of their tasksSam Berry says while some men do not care, a big group - his audience online - "actually are really good husbands, are really good dads, they are trying their best and want to do the best they can, but almost haven't seen it or don't have the language".Many women the BBC spoke to were keen for their partners to take ownership of certain tasks.Sam calls this taking on "a category of tasks" - so dad might handle all the school admin, while mum manages the food.However, he says equality is not necessarily about splitting everything 50/50 - because one partner might work more and another might like cooking - but about finding what works best for both partners.And if you traditionally hold more of the mental load, you might need to accept that your partner may do things very differently, and it might not always go smoothly, says Afua Williams, 40, a mother of two in London.Image source, Afua WilliamsImage caption, Afua Williams says she always has a lot to think about come SeptemberHow to lighten the loadThose who spoke to BBC News shared their own tips about how to manage the mental load equally:Communicate clearly with your partner about how you're feeling and the impact of your mental load. Zach calls it "labelling" - making the invisible cognitive and emotional labour visible. Don't have these conversations when you're feeling angry or overwhelmed, says Wallace, or it can feel like the other person is being "blamed or criticised""See what you can offload", says Ana Catalano Weeks, co-author of a study , externalon how mental load impacts work. Do you really need to organise physical birthday cards for your children's friends? Can you mute parents' WhatsApp groups and just focus on official school emails?Have regular check-ins with your partner - it could be daily, weekly, or seasonallyCreate a shared calendar so that everyone is aware of birthdays, school meetings and moreTake ownership of tasks from start to finish without the need to be reminded, Wallace saysDon't fall into the "efficiency trap" that the solution is just to be more organised, Cleare says. Remember that what matters most as a parent are moments of connection with your child - not eating certain vegetables - and that will help redefine expectations

schema.headline: Why more women carry the 'mental load' - and how couples can share it

title: Dame Prue Leith: 'When you're old, you don't give a toss'
description: Prue Leith: 'You come into your own growing old'Image caption, Dame Prue Leith says growing old is "unstressful" as she prepares to discuss ageing at
body: Prue Leith: 'You come into your own growing old'Image caption, Dame Prue Leith says growing old is "unstressful" as she prepares to discuss ageing at the Cheltenham Literature FestivalByMaisie LillywhiteGloucestershire and Jon SmithBBC Radio Gloucestershire"When you're old, you don't give a toss what anyone thinks, really, so you feel very free. You can have a snooze in the afternoon, and nobody thinks that's odd."Dame Prue Leith is celebrating her perceived joys of the golden years as she prepares to discuss "Growing Old Disgracefully" with fellow authors Gyles Brandreth and Kathy Lette.The trio will take to the stage at this year's Cheltenham Literature Festival on 15 October to prove to the audience ageing is "not the dreaded thing" it is made out to be, the former Bake Off judge said.Dame Prue said: "You come into your own, you don't care what people think, you're not going to change. And so the world has to just put up with it."At 86, the restaurateur and cookery writer has reflected on her younger years and has decided that growing old is good fun, although she acknowledged it may be different for those who are "old and lonely and ill"."When I think of my teenage years, I think they were really stressful," Dame Prue said. "I was always bringing the wrong boys home, and I was quarrelling with my parents, and I didn't know what I wanted to do."I was sort of lost and didn't believe in myself at all... I wanted a boyfriend, couldn't get one, you know. Old age is unstressful."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Dame Prue said she is "very happy" living in the CotswoldsThe talk at The Times and Sunday Times Forum in Montpellier Terrace next month will not be Dame Prue's first time at the festival, which launched in the spa town in 1949.She last appeared at the event in 2018, but outside of her career, she is no stranger to the area."I love Cheltenham; I often go even if I'm not doing anything, but it's a great festival," she said.'I'm very happy here'On screen, Dame Prue showcases her nearby home in Prue Leith's Cotswolds Kitchen, which, she said, gives her an outlet to be "a bossy woman"."I've persuaded my husband to come into it, and he's very funny," she said."It's quite domestic, and it's filmed in our house, so that's even better. It's a great house, and I'm very happy here; I'm in the middle of the Cotswolds. "We built this house four or five years ago, and it's got a great garden... I'm looking out the window as I speak and it's just rolling Cotswolds, fields, can't see a single building."Growing Old Disgracefully will be held at The Times and Sunday Times Forum on 15 October at 13:00.Get in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Gloucestershire
